title: THESIS DEFENSE (NOEL LOO): "Dataset Distillation: Fundamentals and Applications to Privacy"
description: THESIS DEFENSE (NOEL LOO): "Dataset Distillation: Fundamentals and Applications to Privacy" Speaker: Noel LooSpeaker Affiliation: MIT CSAILHost: Daniela RusHost Affiliation: MIT CSAILZoom Link: https://mit.zoom.us/j/5392005602Abstract: One of the central drivers of deep learning's progress has been steadily growing dataset sizes. From the early 2010s to the mid 2020s, dataset sizes have increased by over six orders of magnitude, and models trained on these datasets have consequently improved predictably. This growth brings substantial compute, storage, and privacy costs. These downsides motivate dataset distillation algorithms, which aim to compress datasets into smaller synthetic ones while retaining comparable downstream performance compared to the original dataset. This thesis develops dataset distillation along three frontiers.On the algorithmic front, we develop three algorithms for dataset distillation: RFAD, RCIG, and D3S, each specialized to a different regime of dataset and model size. Through this development, we reveal that a central theme in dataset distillation is tailoring the choice of inner-loop training surrogate to the scale of the downstream model, from an infinite-width kernel approximation at small scale, to a convexified finite-width kernel at moderate scale, to a non-kernel per-layer feature-statistic surrogate at ImageNet scale.On the theoretical front, we make two contributions. Firstly, we prove the first bounds on the sufficient distilled dataset size needed to achieve bounded risk for dataset distillation under Kernel Ridge Regression. Secondly, we provide an empirical analysis showing when the so-called lazy-training regime, which the aforementioned distillation algorithms assume, holds for real finite-width networks.Finally, we use dataset distillation both to understand privacy attacks and to construct privacy-preserving learning algorithms. On the analytic side, we show a formal equivalence between certain training-data reconstruction attacks and the kernel-inducing-point (KIP) family of dataset distillation algorithms. On the constructive side, we present a differentially private dataset distillation algorithm, SPS+, which is competitive with DP-SGD in the fine-tuning regime while offering more flexibility, including unlimited downstream reuse of a single privatized released dataset. Together, these results identify privacy as a compelling motivation for dataset distillation at scale: a single differentially private synthetic dataset can be released once and reused without additional privacy cost across many downstream models.Thesis Committee: Profs. Daniela Rus, Srini Devadas, Antonio Torralba TBD Scaling Multimodal Understanding via Code-Guided Synthetic Data Generation: A Plot Twist Jovana Kondic MIT 3:00 P - 4:00 P Location 45-792
